---
title: "Backends"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

A backend stores {anvl}'s arrays and runs its jitted functions.
There are three:

- `"pjrt"`, the default, compiles with XLA.
- `"quickr"` compiles to Fortran with {quickr}.
- `"r"` runs plain R code and is primarily for testing.

Your code is the same on all three: the same `nv_*` functions and the same `jit()`.
The backends differ in what they need to run, which data types and primitives they support, and how fast they are.

One backend is active at a time.
`local_backend()` sets it until the calling function returns, and `with_backend()` sets it for a single expression:

```{r}
library(anvl)
f <- jit(function(x, y) sum(exp(x) * y))

with_backend("r", {
  x <- nv_array(c(1, 2, 3))
  f(x, x)
})
```

Every array you create and every jitted function you call uses the active backend.
An array belongs to the backend that created it, and using it on another backend is an error.
To move data between backends, convert it with `as_array()` and create a new array with `nv_array()`.

|                       | `"pjrt"`                    | `"quickr"`                      | `"r"`                   |
|-----------------------|-----------------------------|---------------------------------|-------------------------|
| Runs a function as    | an XLA executable           | compiled Fortran                | R code                  |
| Needs                 | a PJRT plugin (downloaded)  | {quickr} and a Fortran compiler | nothing                 |
| Devices               | CPU, CUDA                   | CPU                             | CPU                     |
| Data types            | all                         | `f64`, `i32`, `bool`            | `f64`, `i32`, `bool`    |
| An R double becomes   | `f32`                       | `f64`                           | `f64`                   |
| Primitives            | all                         | a subset                        | the same as `"quickr"`  |
| Meant for             | real work                   | CPU-only, repeated calls        | testing                 |

## pjrt

The default backend traces a function and lowers it to StableHLO.
XLA then compiles it through a PJRT plugin.
It supports every primitive and every data type, and runs on CPU as well as CUDA devices (see `nv_device()`).
Use it for real work.

The plugins are not part of the package.
They are downloaded the first time they are needed, or ahead of time with `install_anvl()` (see the [installation article](installation.html)).

## quickr

The quickr backend lowers the traced graph to an R function instead, built from vectorized R calls and, where needed, loops.
[{quickr}](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/quickr) then translates that function to Fortran and compiles it.
For `f` above, the R function is:

```{r}
graph <- trace_fn(
  function(x, y) sum(exp(x) * y),
  list(x = nv_aval("f64", 3L), y = nv_aval("f64", 3L))
)
cat(deparse(graph_to_quickr_r_function(graph)), sep = "\n")
```

It needs {quickr}, which {anvl} only suggests, and a Fortran compiler.
`install_anvl("quickr")` installs {quickr}.

Arrays live in R's memory as ordinary R arrays, so the CPU is the only device.
Only R's own three storage types are supported: `f64`, `i32` and `bool`.
R has no single precision, so an R double becomes an `f64` array here, while on pjrt it becomes `f32`.
Not every primitive has a quickr rule yet; the [primitives reference](primitives.html) lists which do.

Compiling takes about a second for each function and set of input shapes.
That includes eager code: each operation called outside of `jit()` is compiled the first time it sees new input shapes.
The backend therefore pays off for functions that run many times.

## r

The r backend is primarily for testing, not for real work.
It runs the same R function as quickr, but without compiling it.
It supports the same primitives and data types as quickr and computes the same results.
It needs nothing beyond {anvl} itself: no plugin, no compiler, and no download.
The cost is speed: the program runs as R code, which is fast for vectorized arithmetic but slow wherever the R function loops.

That makes it the backend for tests that cannot rely on a download.
CRAN cannot download a PJRT plugin, so a package that uses {anvl} cannot run its tests there on the default backend.
It can run them on the r backend instead, for example by switching to it in `tests/testthat/setup.R`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
if (!identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true")) {
  anvl::local_backend("r", envir = testthat::teardown_env())
}
```

The tests then run on the r backend on CRAN, and on pjrt everywhere else, locally and on CI.
Two differences between the backends matter for such tests:

- A test that uses a data type other than `f64`, `i32` and `bool`, or a primitive without a quickr rule, must skip on the r backend, e.g. with `skip_if(active_backend() == "r")`.
- An R double becomes `f64` instead of `f32`. A test that checks a data type should compare against `default_float()` rather than `"f32"`.
